title: Mass at The Donmar - ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑ theatre review
transcript: Hello, welcome to Theater Reviews with Paul Semons. I'm here at the Donmar Warehouse to see Mass. Two couples meet after a mass school shooting left both their teenage sons dead. In this play about grief, parental love, anger, and forgiveness, there are depths of emotion that are hard for those of us watching to to take. Um there were moments when I felt I couldn't breathe. That's not to say that the main actors in Fran Kranz's Mass can't lead a play. Uh they can and have, but what is valuable about them in an ensemble play like this is that they don't bring baggage. And that enables you yourself to become immersed in a meeting that seems like a real conversation told verbatim. The encounter takes place 6 years after a school shooting in the US. A deal act as Jay is clearly a civilized liberal man. Um he offers water and worries about recycling, but at times cannot control the animosity he feels. Lindsay Marshall's Gail is an empty shell. Monica Dolan's Linda is so upset at what became of her little boy that her tears seem wrenched from deep inside her. And Paul Hilton's Richard is stiff and defensive but has a downcast face racked with sorrow. The two mothers are especially moving when they remember their sons as young children. It's essential to the maintaining the tension that there is no breaking continuity in Carrie Cracknell's impeccable production. So, the participants remain seated for nearly the whole exchange. And that's rare in itself because so many productions that you see, it seems like the actors have been made to walk up and down just to keep it interesting. Consequently, to avoid us having to look at the back of someone's head the whole time, there is a revolve that moves imperceptibly but turns them round so that we get to see all their faces. And all the pain they are expressing. The play is set in the meeting room of a church, ironically a soulless piece of modern architecture with lots of glass and light but no human touch. And this is expertly conjured by designer Anna Yates who shows us the kitchen and corridors and stairs outside the room. This is not a play of despair. Uh yes, Fran Kranz who made the 2020 film on which this is based examines reactions to tragedy but he also explores the concept of restorative justice. And this is where the play takes on a greater dimension. We may not live in the USA. Mass killings are far less common here uh in the UK, but they do happen nevertheless. And we are also part of a world in which war and terrorism breed more of the same. And at an individual level, people cope with the results of knife attacks, dangerous driving, and more. All over the world and throughout history, loss has left people seeking retribution. The resultant and revenge can destroy us. Reconciliation where the perpetrators admit their guilt and the victims forgive offers hope that instead of being consumed by grief, the parents can live alongside it. There's no sense that this isn't easy or a complete answer, but the understanding the couples gain about each other in the course of the play offers at least the prospect of peace. The play has a kind of prologue and epilogue in which the characters played by Amari Bakar Rochelle Rose and Susie Trailing prepare for the meeting and clear up afterwards. I cannot stress how important this is as a play. Frank Krenz, Carrie Cracknell, and this extraordinary cast have given us an insight into the anguish of loss and the possibility of hope.
